bricks.title: Regional Anatomy of the Posterior Abdominal Wall, Back, and Posterior Neck

items.why: PAW skeletal framework: lumbar vertebrae, 12th rib, pelvis, proximal femur

questions.q: The iliopsoas runs from the lumbar vertebrae and iliac fossa to which attachment?
questions.explain: The iliopsoas extends from the lumbar vertebrae and iliac fossa to the lesser trochanter of the femur.

items.excerpt: The posterior abdominal wall is supported by the lumbar vertebrae, twelfth rib, pelvis, and proximal femur.

items.why: Iliopsoas: primary hip flexor; psoas L1-L3 anterior rami, iliacus femoral n.; psoas abscess/hematoma

questions.q: Which muscle of the posterior abdominal wall is the primary flexor of the hip?
questions.explain: The iliopsoas (psoas major and iliacus) is the primary hip flexor; quadratus lumborum stabilizes the 12th rib and laterally flexes the spine.

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the iliacus?
questions.explain: The iliacus is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4), whereas psoas major is supplied directly by anterior rami of L1-L3.

questions.q: A patient with tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) develops fever, back pain, and holds the hip slightly flexed. Infection has most likely spread into which compartment?
questions.explain: In Pott disease, vertebral infection can spread into the psoas compartment, producing a psoas abscess; patients hold the hip flexed to avoid stretching the muscle.

items.excerpt: Extending from the lumbar vertebrae and iliac fossa to the lesser trochanter of the femur, it is the primary flexor of the hip…

items.why: Quadratus lumborum: iliac crest to 12th rib/lumbar TPs; stabilizes 12th rib, ipsilateral lateral flexion; T12-L4

questions.q: What is the primary action of the quadratus lumborum?
choices: Ipsilateral lateral flexion of the spine
questions.explain: Quadratus lumborum stabilizes (fixes) the 12th rib during respiration and produces ipsilateral lateral flexion of the vertebral column.

questions.q: The quadratus lumborum is innervated by which nerves?
questions.explain: Like the other posterior abdominal wall muscles, quadratus lumborum is supplied by anterior rami (T12-L4).

items.excerpt: It stabilizes the twelfth rib during respiration and produces ipsilateral lateral flexion of the vertebral column.

items.why: Trapezius: CN XI motor; transverse cervical a.; elevates, retracts, depresses, upwardly rotates scapula

questions.q: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the trapezius?
questions.explain: The trapezius is the exception among extrinsic back muscles: motor supply is CN XI, with C3-C4 carrying sensory/proprioceptive fibers.

questions.q: Which artery is the main blood supply of the trapezius?
questions.explain: Table 3 lists the transverse cervical artery as the blood supply of the trapezius.

items.excerpt: The trapezius is an exception, receiving motor innervation from the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).

items.why: Latissimus dorsi: thoracodorsal n. and a.; extends, adducts, medially rotates arm

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the latissimus dorsi?
questions.explain: Latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve and thoracodorsal artery.

questions.q: Which set of arm movements does the latissimus dorsi produce?
questions.explain: Latissimus dorsi extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm (e.g., climbing and pulling).

items.excerpt: Latissimus dorsi: Thoracodorsal nerve; Thoracodorsal artery; Extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm

items.why: Levator scapulae: dorsal scapular n./a.; elevates scapula

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the levator scapulae?
questions.explain: Levator scapulae is supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and artery and elevates the scapula.

items.excerpt: Levator scapulae: Dorsal scapular nerve; Dorsal scapular artery; Elevates the scapula

items.why: Rhomboid major: dorsal scapular n.; retracts and stabilizes scapula

questions.q: What is the primary action of rhomboid major?
questions.explain: Rhomboid major and minor retract and stabilize the scapula; they are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve.

items.excerpt: Rhomboid major & minor: Dorsal scapular nerve; Dorsal scapular artery; Retracts and stabilizes the scapula

items.why: Rhomboid minor: dorsal scapular n./a.; retracts scapula

questions.q: Which artery supplies rhomboid minor?
questions.explain: Both rhomboids (and levator scapulae) are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and dorsal scapular artery.

items.excerpt: The superficial extrinsic back muscles include the trapezius, latissimus dorsi, levator scapulae, and rhomboid major and minor

items.why: Serratus posterior sup/inf: intermediate extrinsic; intercostal nn.; mainly proprioceptive

questions.q: Although classed as accessory respiratory muscles, the serratus posterior muscles are thought to function mainly in what?
questions.explain: The serratus posterior superior and inferior play only a minor role in breathing and are thought to contribute primarily to proprioception.

questions.q: Serratus posterior inferior is innervated by which nerves?
questions.explain: Serratus posterior superior is supplied by intercostal nerves T2-T5 and serratus posterior inferior by T9-T12.

items.excerpt: …they play only a minor role in breathing and are thought to contribute primarily to proprioception.

items.why: Anterior rami: supply extrinsic back and posterior abdominal wall muscles

questions.q: The extrinsic back muscles (except trapezius) are innervated primarily by which branches?
questions.explain: Extrinsic back muscles are supplied mainly by anterior rami, reflecting their embryologic link with limb musculature.

items.excerpt: …they are innervated primarily by anterior rami of spinal nerves, reflecting their embryologic association with the limb musculature.

items.why: Typical vertebra: body anterior, vertebral arch posterior (pedicles + laminae)

questions.q: The vertebral arch of a typical vertebra is formed by which paired parts?
questions.explain: A typical vertebra has a body anteriorly and a vertebral arch posteriorly formed by paired pedicles and laminae.

items.excerpt: A typical vertebra consists of a body anteriorly and a vertebral arch posteriorly.

items.why: Pedicle: part of arch; vertebral notches of adjacent pedicles form intervertebral foramen

questions.q: The superior and inferior vertebral notches of adjacent pedicles form which opening?
questions.explain: Each intervertebral foramen is formed in part by the vertebral notches of adjacent pedicles; spinal nerves exit through it.

items.excerpt: Each intervertebral foramen is formed in part by the superior and inferior vertebral notches of adjacent pedicles.

items.why: Lamina: posterior part of arch between transverse and spinous processes

questions.q: Which part of a vertebra forms the posterior arch between the transverse and spinous processes?
questions.explain: The laminae form the posterior portion of the vertebral arch, between the transverse process and the spinous process.

items.excerpt: Which part of a typical vertebra forms the posterior portion of the vertebral arch between the transverse process and spinous process?

items.why: Vertebral foramen: surrounded by body + arch; stacked foramina form vertebral canal

questions.q: Successive vertebral foramina together form what structure?
questions.explain: The body and arch surround the vertebral foramen; the vertebral foramina of successive vertebrae form the vertebral canal.

items.excerpt: The vertebral arch is formed by paired pedicles and laminae and, together with the body, surrounds the vertebral foramen.

items.why: Vertebral canal: formed by stacked vertebral foramina; houses the spinal cord
items.excerpt: The vertebral foramina of successive vertebrae collectively form the vertebral canal.

items.why: Spinous process: back muscle/ligament attachment; C7 vertebra prominens is a palpable landmark

questions.q: Which spinous process is usually easily palpable at the base of the neck and used to count vertebral levels?
questions.explain: The spinous process of C7 (vertebra prominens) is a key palpable landmark at the base of the neck.

items.excerpt: The spinous process of C7 (vertebra prominens) is usually easily palpable at the base of the neck…

items.why: Transverse process: attachment site; QL attaches to TPs of upper lumbar vertebrae

questions.q: The quadratus lumborum attaches superiorly to the twelfth rib and to which vertebral feature?
choices: Spinous processes of upper lumbar vertebrae
Transverse processes of upper lumbar vertebrae
Bodies of the lower thoracic vertebrae
Laminae of the lower lumbar vertebrae
questions.explain: Quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament to the 12th rib and the transverse processes of the upper lumbar vertebrae.

items.excerpt: The spinous and transverse processes provide important attachment sites for the muscles and ligaments of the back.

items.why: Intervertebral foramen: spinal nerves exit the vertebral canal

questions.q: What passes through the intervertebral foramina?
questions.explain: Spinal nerves exit the vertebral canal through the intervertebral foramina, which lie between adjacent vertebrae.

items.excerpt: The intervertebral foramina are openings between adjacent vertebrae through which spinal nerves exit the vertebral canal.

items.why: Cervical vertebra: identified by transverse foramina

questions.q: Which feature is characteristic of cervical vertebrae?
questions.explain: Cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina; thoracic vertebrae have rib facets; lumbar vertebrae have large bodies.

items.excerpt: Cervical vertebrae are characterized by transverse foramina.

items.why: Transverse foramen: transmits the vertebral artery, usually entering at C6

questions.q: At which level does the vertebral artery typically enter the transverse foramina?
questions.explain: The vertebral arteries typically enter the transverse foramina at C6 and ascend to the atlas before entering the skull through the foramen magnum.

items.excerpt: The vertebral arteries ascend through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae, typically entering at the level of C6…

items.why: Vertebral artery: ascends in transverse foramina, enters skull via foramen magnum; compression -> vertigo, ataxia

questions.q: Osteophytes and extreme neck rotation compress a vertebral artery. Which presentation is most expected?
choices: Wrist drop and dorsal hand numbness
questions.explain: Vertebral artery compression reduces flow to the brainstem, cerebellum, and occipital lobes, causing dizziness, vertigo, ataxia, visual disturbances, or syncope.

questions.q: The vertebral artery enters the cranial cavity through which opening?
questions.explain: After ascending through the cervical transverse foramina to C1, the vertebral artery enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum.

items.excerpt: …can injure or compress a vertebral artery, reducing blood flow to the brainstem, cerebellum, and occipital lobes.

items.why: Thoracic vertebra: facets for rib articulation

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes thoracic vertebrae?
questions.explain: Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets for articulation with the ribs.

items.excerpt: Thoracic vertebrae have facets for articulation with the ribs.

items.why: Costal facets: rib articulations on thoracic vertebrae
items.excerpt: Thoracic vertebrae have facets for articulation with the ribs.

items.why: Lumbar vertebra: large bodies to bear greater weight

questions.q: Why are lumbar vertebral bodies so large?
choices: To allow rotation of the head
questions.explain: Lumbar vertebrae have large vertebral bodies adapted to support greater weight.

items.excerpt: Lumbar vertebrae have large vertebral bodies adapted to support greater weight.

items.why: Atlas (C1): no body or typical spinous process; atlanto-occipital joint with occipital condyles

questions.q: Which vertebra lacks a body and articulates with the occipital condyles?
questions.explain: The atlas lacks a body and a typical spinous process and articulates with the occipital condyles at the atlanto-occipital joints.

items.excerpt: The atlas (C1) lacks a body and a typical spinous process and articulates superiorly with the occipital condyles at the atlanto-occipital joints.

items.why: Axis (C2) and dens: pivot for head rotation at the atlantoaxial joint

questions.q: The dens of the axis is the pivot for which movement?
questions.explain: The dens projects superiorly and is the pivot around which the atlas and head rotate at the atlantoaxial joint.

items.excerpt: The axis (C2) is distinguished by the dens, which projects superiorly and provides a pivot around which the atlas and head rotate…

items.why: Posterior rami: innervate all intrinsic back muscles

questions.q: Intrinsic back muscles such as the erector spinae and multifidus are supplied by which branches?
questions.explain: The intrinsic back muscles are innervated by posterior (dorsal) rami of spinal nerves.

items.excerpt: They primarily move and stabilize the vertebral column and head and are innervated by the posterior (dorsal) rami of spinal nerves.

items.why: Splenius capitis/cervicis: most superficial intrinsic layer of neck; ipsilateral rotation; cervical posterior rami

questions.q: Acting unilaterally, the splenius muscles rotate the head in which way?
questions.explain: Bilaterally the splenius capitis and cervicis extend the head and neck; unilaterally they laterally flex and rotate it to the same side.

questions.q: The splenius muscles are innervated by which nerves?
questions.explain: As intrinsic back muscles, the splenius muscles are supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami of cervical spinal nerves.

items.excerpt: The splenius capitis and splenius cervicis form the most superficial layer of the intrinsic back muscles in the posterior neck

items.why: Erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis): largest intrinsic group; extends spine, posture; posterior rami

questions.q: A 68-year-old man has weak vertebral column extension and trouble maintaining upright posture, with normal scapular movement. Which muscle group is most likely affected?
questions.explain: The erector spinae is the largest intrinsic back group; it extends and laterally flexes the spine and maintains upright posture.

questions.q: Which nerves innervate the erector spinae?
questions.explain: All intrinsic back muscles, including the erector spinae, are supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami.

items.excerpt: The erector spinae is the largest intrinsic back muscle group and consists of the iliocostalis, longissimus, and spinalis muscles

items.why: Transversospinalis (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores): deep to erector spinae; stabilizes, contralateral rotation

questions.q: Which intrinsic back group lies deep to the erector spinae and assists contralateral rotation of the spine?
questions.explain: The transversospinalis group sits in the groove between transverse and spinous processes, stabilizes adjacent vertebrae, and assists extension and contralateral rotation.

items.excerpt: These muscles stabilize adjacent vertebrae and assist with extension and contralateral rotation of the vertebral column.

items.why: Semispinalis: transversospinalis muscle; suboccipital muscles lie beneath semispinalis capitis

questions.q: The suboccipital muscles lie directly deep to which muscle?
questions.explain: The suboccipital muscles lie deep in the posterior neck beneath the semispinalis capitis, a transversospinalis muscle.

items.excerpt: These muscles lie deep in the posterior neck beneath the semispinalis capitis.

items.why: Multifidus: transversospinalis; key stabilizer of lumbar spine; implicated in mechanical LBP

questions.q: Which transversospinalis muscle is particularly important for stabilizing the lumbar spine?
questions.explain: The multifidus is particularly important for lumbar stability; its weakness contributes to mechanical low back pain.

items.excerpt: The multifidus is particularly important for stabilizing the lumbar spine during movement.

items.why: Suboccipital triangle: RCP major + obliquus sup/inf; contains vertebral a. and suboccipital n.

questions.q: Which structures lie within the suboccipital triangle?
choices: Deep cervical artery and C2 root
questions.explain: The triangle bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis superior and inferior contains the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve.

questions.q: The suboccipital muscles are innervated by which nerve?
questions.explain: The suboccipital nerve is the posterior ramus of C1; these muscles fine-tune movement at the atlanto-occipital and atlantoaxial joints.

items.excerpt: …3 muscles bounding the suboccipital triangle containing the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve

items.why: SCM: manubrium/clavicle to mastoid; CN XI; unilateral contralateral rotation; torticollis

questions.q: Acting unilaterally, the sternocleidomastoid turns the head in which way?
questions.explain: Unilaterally the SCM laterally flexes the neck and rotates the head to the opposite side; bilaterally it flexes the neck.

questions.q: An infant's head is tilted toward the left with the chin rotated to the right because of fibrosis of a neck muscle. Which condition is this?
questions.explain: Torticollis is shortening of the SCM, tilting the head toward the affected side and rotating it away; it is often treated with stretching in infancy.

questions.q: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid?
questions.explain: Like the trapezius, the SCM receives motor innervation from CN XI; C2-C3 carry sensory/proprioceptive fibers.

items.excerpt: Acting unilaterally, it laterally flexes the neck and rotates the head to the opposite side.

items.why: Mastoid process: superior attachment of SCM

questions.q: Which muscle attaches to the mastoid process of the temporal bone?
questions.explain: The sternocleidomastoid extends from the manubrium and clavicle to the mastoid process.

items.excerpt: The sternocleidomastoid … extends from the manubrium and clavicle to the mastoid process of the temporal bone.

items.why: Posterior triangle: SCM is anterior boundary; contains CN XI, brachial plexus roots, EJV

questions.q: Which muscle forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explain: The SCM is the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle, which contains CN XI, roots of the brachial plexus, and the external jugular vein.

questions.q: Which of these lies in the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explain: The posterior triangle contains the spinal accessory nerve, the roots of the brachial plexus, and the external jugular vein.

items.excerpt: It is the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle, where the spinal accessory nerve, roots of the brachial plexus, and the external jugular vein…

items.why: Manubrium: inferior (sternal) attachment of SCM
items.excerpt: The sternocleidomastoid … extends from the manubrium and clavicle to the mastoid process of the temporal bone.

items.why: Clavicle: inferior (clavicular) attachment of SCM
items.excerpt: The sternocleidomastoid … extends from the manubrium and clavicle to the mastoid process of the temporal bone.

groups.title: Skeletal Framework of the Vertebral Column

items.why: Spinal cord regions: 31 pairs (C8, T12, L5, S5, Co1); C1-C7 exit above, others below their vertebrae

questions.q: How many pairs of spinal nerves arise from the cervical spinal cord?
questions.explain: There are 8 cervical nerve pairs but only 7 cervical vertebrae; in total there are 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

questions.q: Which spinal nerve exits above the T1 vertebra?
questions.explain: C1-C7 exit above their vertebrae; there is no C8 vertebra, so C8 exits above T1 and thoracic and lower nerves exit below their vertebrae.

items.excerpt: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves grouped into five regions: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal

items.why: Posterior root: sensory fibers enter; cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia

questions.q: Where are the cell bodies of the sensory fibers in the posterior (dorsal) root?
questions.explain: Sensory fibers enter through the posterior roots; their primary sensory neuron cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglia.

items.excerpt: At each segment, sensory fibers enter the spinal cord through the posterior (dorsal) roots, while motor fibers leave through the anterior (ventral) roots.

items.why: Anterior root: motor fibers (somatic and preganglionic autonomic) leave the cord

questions.q: Axons of ventral horn somatic motor neurons leave the spinal cord through which structure?
questions.explain: Motor fibers, including preganglionic autonomic axons from the lateral horn, leave the cord through the anterior roots.

items.excerpt: Axons from these autonomic motor neurons leave the spinal cord through the ventral roots before traveling to autonomic ganglia.

items.why: Spinal nerve: mixed nerve formed by posterior + anterior roots; exits via intervertebral foramen

questions.q: Which statement best describes a spinal nerve?
choices: Mixed nerve formed by both roots
Purely sensory branch of the cord
Purely motor branch of the cord
questions.explain: The posterior and anterior roots join to form a mixed spinal nerve, which leaves through the intervertebral foramen and splits into rami.

items.excerpt: The posterior and anterior roots join to form a mixed spinal nerve that connects the spinal cord with the periphery…

items.why: Posterior ramus: mixed primary ramus of the spinal nerve
items.excerpt: …connects the spinal cord with the periphery through mixed dorsal (posterior) and ventral (anterior) primary rami.

items.why: Anterior ramus: mixed primary ramus of the spinal nerve
items.excerpt: …are distributed through the dorsal and ventral primary rami to innervate skeletal muscles of the back, trunk, and limbs

items.why: Conus medullaris: tapered end of cord at about L1-L2 in adults

questions.q: In adults, the spinal cord tapers into the conus medullaris at about which vertebral level?
questions.explain: In adults the cord extends from the foramen magnum to about L1-L2, where it ends as the conus medullaris.

items.excerpt: In adults, the spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum to approximately the L1–L2 vertebral level, where it tapers to form the conus medullaris.

items.why: Cauda equina: lumbar, sacral, coccygeal roots descending below the conus

questions.q: Why do lower spinal nerve roots descend within the vertebral canal as the cauda equina?
choices: The roots must pass through the dura
The cord ends at the coccyx in adults
The vertebral column outgrows the cord
The roots join the brachial plexus
questions.explain: Because the vertebral column grows faster than the cord, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal roots descend before exiting, forming the cauda equina.

items.excerpt: In adults, the spinal cord typically ends at the L1-L2 vertebral level as the conus medullaris; spinal nerve roots continuing inferiorly form the cauda equina.

items.why: Dura mater: outermost meninx; puncture -> CSF leak, post-dural puncture headache

questions.q: What is the correct order of the spinal meninges from superficial to deep?
questions.explain: The dura mater is most external, the arachnoid mater is the middle layer, and the pia mater is most internal.

questions.q: During epidural anesthesia, accidental puncture of the dura mater most likely causes which complication?
questions.explain: Puncturing the dura can let CSF leak, producing a post-dural puncture headache.

items.excerpt: Accidental puncture of the dura mater may result in leakage of cerebrospinal fluid and a post-dural puncture headache.

items.why: Arachnoid mater: middle meninx; subarachnoid space lies deep to it

questions.q: CSF lies between the arachnoid mater and which other layer?
questions.explain: The subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and pia mater, contains cerebrospinal fluid.

items.excerpt: Between the arachnoid and pia mater is the subarachnoid space, which contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

items.why: Pia mater: innermost meninx, directly on the cord
items.excerpt: The meninges are composed of three layers … Pia mater (most internal)

items.why: Epidural space: real space with fat, vessels, lymphatics; site of epidural anesthesia

questions.q: Epidural anesthetic for labor is injected into a space containing which contents?
questions.explain: The spinal epidural space, outside the dura, contains epidural fat, blood vessels, and lymphatics; anesthetic there bathes the spinal nerve roots.

questions.q: How does the spinal epidural space differ from the cranial epidural space?
choices: Spinal is a real space; cranial is potential
Spinal is potential; cranial is a real space
Both are filled with cerebrospinal fluid
Both lie between arachnoid and pia
questions.explain: In the vertebral canal the epidural space is an actual space filled with fat; around the brain it is only a potential space between skull and dura.

items.excerpt: Within the vertebral column, the epidural space of the spinal cord is an actual space occupied by the epidural fat.

items.why: Subarachnoid space: between arachnoid and pia; contains CSF

questions.q: Which space contains cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.explain: The subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and pia mater, contains CSF.

items.excerpt: The subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid mater and pia mater, contains cerebrospinal fluid.

items.why: Lumbar cistern: enlarged subarachnoid space below conus; LP at L3-L4/L4-L5

questions.q: A lumbar puncture is commonly performed between which vertebrae?
questions.explain: Because the cord ends at L1-L2, the needle is placed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 into the lumbar cistern, where cauda equina roots float in CSF.

questions.q: During a lumbar puncture, which ligament is the last one pierced before the vertebral canal is entered?
questions.explain: The needle passes the supraspinous ligament, then the interspinous ligament, then the ligamentum flavum before entering the vertebral canal.

items.excerpt: Inferior to the conus medullaris, the subarachnoid space enlarges to form the lumbar cistern, which contains CSF and the nerve roots of the cauda equina.

items.why: Vertebral canal: houses the spinal cord
items.excerpt: The spinal cord is a tubular structure of nervous tissue that … extends caudally within the vertebral canal.

items.why: Vertebral foramina stack to form the vertebral canal
items.excerpt: As described in the regional anatomy of the back, successive vertebral foramina form the vertebral canal.

items.why: Intervertebral foramina: exit of spinal nerves
items.excerpt: Spinal nerve roots extend from the spinal cord and join to form spinal nerves, which leave the vertebral column through the intervertebral foramina

bricks.title: Functional Anatomy of the Shoulder & Arm

items.why: Clavicle: strut holding limb from thorax; SC joint medially, AC joint laterally

questions.q: What is the main mechanical role of the clavicle?
choices: A socket for the head of the humerus
A strut holding the limb off the thorax
Origin of the rotator cuff muscles
Attachment of the long head of biceps
questions.explain: The clavicle acts as a strut that holds the upper limb away from the thoracic wall, articulating with the sternum medially and the acromion laterally.

items.excerpt: The clavicle acts as a strut that holds the upper limb away from the thoracic wall, allowing greater freedom of movement.

items.why: Sternum: medial articulation of the clavicle (SC joint)
items.excerpt: Medially, it articulates with the sternum at the sternoclavicular joint.

items.why: Scapula: flat triangular bone on the posterior thoracic wall
items.excerpt: The scapula is a flat triangular bone located on the posterior thoracic wall.

items.why: Spine of scapula: divides posterior surface into supra/infraspinous fossae; expands as acromion

questions.q: The spine of the scapula expands laterally to form which feature?
questions.explain: The scapular spine divides the posterior surface into the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae and expands laterally as the acromion.

items.excerpt: The spine of the scapula divides its posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.

items.why: Supraspinous fossa: home of supraspinatus, which initiates abduction

questions.q: The muscle filling the supraspinous fossa is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explain: Supraspinatus (in the supraspinous fossa) initiates abduction and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve.

items.excerpt: The spine of the scapula divides its posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.

items.why: Infraspinous fossa: home of infraspinatus (lateral rotation, suprascapular n.)

questions.q: The muscle filling the infraspinous fossa mainly produces which movement?
questions.explain: Infraspinatus, in the infraspinous fossa, laterally rotates the humerus and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve.

items.excerpt: The spine of the scapula divides its posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.

items.why: Acromion: forms AC joint; supraspinatus tendon passes beneath it (impingement)

questions.q: Which tendon passes beneath the acromion and is most often torn in rotator cuff injury?
questions.explain: The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath the acromion and coracoacromial arch to the greater tubercle, making it vulnerable to impingement and tears.

items.excerpt: The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath the acromion before inserting on the greater tubercle of the humerus.

items.why: Coracoid process: origin of short head of biceps and coracobrachialis; part of CA arch

questions.q: Which muscle arises from the coracoid process?
questions.explain: The short head of biceps and the coracobrachialis arise from the coracoid process; the long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle.

items.excerpt: The coracoid process projects anteriorly and serves as an attachment site for several muscles and ligaments.

items.why: Glenoid cavity: articulates with humeral head to form GH joint

questions.q: The glenoid cavity articulates with which structure?
questions.explain: The glenoid cavity articulates with the head of the humerus to form the glenohumeral joint.

items.excerpt: The glenoid cavity articulates with the head of the humerus to form the glenohumeral joint.

items.why: Suprascapular n.: under superior transverse scapular ligament ('Navy under the bridge')

questions.q: At the suprascapular notch, how does the suprascapular nerve relate to the superior transverse scapular ligament?
choices: It runs lateral to the notch
questions.explain: 'Army over the bridge, Navy under': the artery passes above the ligament and the nerve passes beneath it.

items.excerpt: The suprascapular notch … transmits the suprascapular nerve beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament, while the suprascapular artery passes above the ligament.

items.why: Humerus: single long bone of the arm
items.excerpt: The arm extends from the shoulder to the elbow and contains a single long bone, the humerus.

items.why: Head of humerus: articulates with glenoid cavity
items.excerpt: The glenohumeral joint is a ball and socket synovial joint formed by the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula.

items.why: Anatomical neck: part of the proximal humerus
items.excerpt: The proximal humerus includes the head, anatomical neck, greater and lesser tubercles, intertubercular groove, and surgical neck.

questions.explain: Lumbricals and interossei flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints.

items.excerpt: Together, they flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints, allowing the fingers to conform to objects of different shapes.

items.why: IP joints: FDS flexes PIP, FDP flexes DIP; claw = IP flexion

questions.q: In an ulnar claw deformity, what is the position of the interphalangeal joints of digits 4 and 5?
questions.explain: Ulnar claw shows MCP hyperextension with IP flexion, most marked in digits 4 and 5.

items.excerpt: The deformity is characterized by hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion of the interphalangeal joints…

bricks.title: Functional Anatomy of the Gluteal Region, Hip, Thigh & Knee

items.why: Iliac crest ends anteriorly at ASIS; attachment landmarks

questions.q: The iliac crest terminates anteriorly at which landmark?
questions.explain: The superior border of the ilium forms the iliac crest, which ends anteriorly at the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).

items.excerpt: The superior border of the ilium forms the iliac crest, which terminates anteriorly at the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).

items.why: Ischial tuberosity: posterior thigh (hamstring) attachment; bears weight when sitting

questions.q: Which bony landmark bears weight when sitting and anchors the posterior thigh muscles?
questions.explain: The ischial tuberosity bears weight when sitting and is the attachment site for the hamstring muscles of the posterior thigh.

items.excerpt: Inferiorly, the ischial tuberosity provides an important attachment site for muscles of the posterior thigh and bears weight when sitting.

items.why: Pubis: one of three bones fusing to form the hip bone
items.excerpt: Each hip bone is formed by three bones: the ilium, ischium, and pubis, which fuse during development.

items.why: Acetabulum: deep socket for femoral head; more bony stability than the glenoid

questions.q: Which three bones meet at the acetabulum?
questions.explain: The ilium, ischium, and pubis fuse during development and meet at the acetabulum, the socket for the femoral head.

questions.q: What gives the hip joint greater inherent stability than the shoulder joint?
choices: A capsule reinforced by rotator cuff
questions.explain: The acetabulum forms a deep socket around the femoral head, providing more bony stability than the shallow glenoid cavity.

items.excerpt: The acetabulum forms a deep socket around the head of the femur, providing greater bony stability than the relatively shallow glenoid cavity of the shoulder.

items.why: Femoral head articulates with acetabulum; neck fracture -> avascular necrosis

questions.q: An older woman sustains a femoral neck fracture. Which complication is of particular concern?
questions.explain: Femoral neck fractures can disrupt vessels supplying the femoral head, producing avascular necrosis, a particular concern in older adults.

items.excerpt: A fracture of the femoral neck can disrupt blood vessels that supply the femoral head.

items.why: Greater trochanter: gluteus medius/minimus insertion; lesser trochanter: iliopsoas

questions.q: Which muscle inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur?
questions.explain: The lesser trochanter is the attachment site for the primary hip flexor, the iliopsoas.

questions.q: The gluteus medius and gluteus minimus insert on which landmark?
questions.explain: Gluteus medius and minimus insert on the greater trochanter, which lets them abduct and medially rotate the thigh.

items.excerpt: The smaller lesser trochanter projects from the posteromedial femur and serves as an attachment site for the primary hip flexor.

items.why: Acetabular labrum: fibrocartilage ring deepening the socket

questions.q: What is the main function of the acetabular labrum?
choices: Deepens the socket to add stability
Carries blood to the femoral head
Anchors the ligament of the head
questions.explain: The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilage ring on the acetabular rim that deepens the socket and adds stability; the iliofemoral ligament limits extension.

items.excerpt: The acetabular labrum, a ring of fibrocartilage attached to the rim of the acetabulum, deepens the socket and further contributes to joint stability.

items.why: Gmax: hip extension + lateral rotation (inferior gluteal n.); Gmed/min: abduct, medially rotate (superior gluteal n.)

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the gluteus maximus?
questions.explain: The gluteus maximus, the primary hip extensor, is innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve.

questions.q: Besides abducting the thigh, gluteus medius and gluteus minimus produce which movement?
questions.explain: Inserting on the greater trochanter, gluteus medius and minimus abduct and medially rotate the thigh.

questions.q: Standing on her right leg, a patient's pelvis drops on the left side. Weakness of which muscles explains this?
questions.explain: The abductors on the weight-bearing side keep the pelvis from dropping toward the unsupported side; right gluteus medius/minimus weakness gives a Trendelenburg sign.

items.excerpt: The gluteus maximus is the primary gluteal muscle responsible for extension of the hip and also contributes to lateral rotation of the thigh

items.why: Inferior gluteal n. -> gluteus maximus (hip extension, propulsion)

questions.q: Injury to the inferior gluteal nerve would most weaken which activity?
questions.explain: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, which extends the hip and works with the hamstrings for propulsion such as climbing stairs.

items.excerpt: The gluteus maximus is innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve.

items.why: TFL: abducts, medially rotates, assists hip flexion; superior gluteal n.

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the tensor fasciae latae?
questions.explain: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae are all innervated by the superior gluteal nerve.

questions.q: In addition to abducting the thigh, the tensor fasciae latae assists with which hip movement?
questions.explain: The tensor fasciae latae abducts and medially rotates the thigh and assists with hip flexion.

items.excerpt: The gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae work together to abduct the thigh and stabilize the pelvis during walking

items.why: Superior gluteal n. injury -> Gmed/Gmin weakness -> Trendelenburg gait

questions.q: Which nerve injury is most likely in a patient with a positive Trendelenburg sign?
questions.explain: Superior gluteal nerve injury weakens gluteus medius and minimus, so the pelvis drops toward the unsupported side (Trendelenburg sign).

questions.q: After right hip surgery, a patient's pelvis drops on the left when she stands on her right leg, and she leans her trunk right. Which nerve is injured?
questions.explain: The right superior gluteal nerve supplies the right hip abductors that hold the pelvis level during right single-leg stance; patients compensate by leaning toward the affected side.

items.excerpt: Weakness of these muscles or injury to the superior gluteal nerve can therefore produce an abnormal Trendelenburg gait.

items.why: Piriformis: lateral rotator; sciatic n. exits inferior to it; piriformis syndrome

questions.q: Gluteal pain radiating into the posterior thigh, worse with prolonged sitting, suggests the piriformis is compressing which nerve?
questions.explain: In piriformis syndrome the piriformis irritates or compresses the sciatic nerve as it exits the pelvis, causing gluteal pain radiating to the posterior thigh.

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the piriformis?
questions.explain: The piriformis is supplied by the nerve to piriformis, one of the small sacral plexus branches to the deep rotators.

questions.q: Piriformis and obturator internus laterally rotate the extended thigh. Which action do they assist when the hip is flexed?
questions.explain: The piriformis and obturator internus can also assist with abduction when the hip is flexed.

items.excerpt: Piriformis syndrome occurs when the piriformis irritates or compresses the sciatic nerve as it exits the pelvis.

items.why: Obturator internus: lateral rotation; abducts flexed thigh; nerve to obturator internus

questions.q: What is the primary action of the obturator internus?
questions.explain: The deep external rotators, including obturator internus, primarily laterally rotate the thigh and stabilize the femoral head in the acetabulum.

items.excerpt: The piriformis and obturator internus can also assist with abduction when the hip is flexed.

items.why: Gemelli: lateral rotators; superior = n. to obturator internus, inferior = n. to quadratus femoris

questions.q: Which nerves supply the superior and inferior gemelli, respectively?
choices: N. to quadratus femoris; n. to obturator internus
N. to piriformis; inferior gluteal nerve
N. to obturator internus; n. to quadratus femoris
Obturator nerve; n. to obturator internus
questions.explain: The superior gemellus travels with obturator internus (nerve to obturator internus); the inferior gemellus with quadratus femoris (nerve to quadratus femoris).

items.excerpt: The nerve to obturator internus innervates the obturator internus and superior gemellus, while the nerve to quadratus femoris innervates the quadratus femoris and inferior gemellus.

items.why: Quadratus femoris: lateral rotator; nerve to quadratus femoris

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the quadratus femoris?
questions.explain: The nerve to quadratus femoris supplies the quadratus femoris and the inferior gemellus.

items.excerpt: …a group of smaller muscles that primarily laterally rotate the thigh and stabilize the head of the femur within the acetabulum.

items.why: Obturator externus: lateral rotator, the exception innervated by the obturator n.

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the obturator externus?
questions.explain: Unlike the other deep external rotators (sacral plexus branches), the obturator externus is innervated by the obturator nerve.

questions.q: Although grouped with the medial thigh, the obturator externus's primary action is which?
choices: Adduction of the thigh at hip
Extension of the thigh at the hip
questions.explain: The obturator externus differs from the other medial compartment muscles because its primary action is lateral rotation of the thigh.

items.excerpt: The obturator externus is an exception and is innervated by the obturator nerve.

items.why: Greater sciatic foramen: sciatic n. exits inferior to piriformis

questions.q: The sciatic nerve typically exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen in what relation to the piriformis?
questions.explain: The piriformis is the landmark of the greater sciatic foramen; the sciatic nerve typically exits inferior to it.

items.excerpt: The sciatic nerve typically exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen inferior to the piriformis before descending into the posterior thigh.

items.why: Nerve to piriformis: small sacral plexus branch (Table 1)
items.excerpt: The deep external rotators receive innervation from several small branches of the sacral plexus.

items.why: Nerve to obturator internus: obturator internus + superior gemellus

questions.q: Besides the obturator internus, which muscle does the nerve to obturator internus supply?
questions.explain: The nerve to obturator internus supplies the obturator internus and the superior gemellus.

items.excerpt: The nerve to obturator internus innervates the obturator internus and superior gemellus…

items.why: Nerve to quadratus femoris: quadratus femoris + inferior gemellus
items.excerpt: …the nerve to quadratus femoris innervates the quadratus femoris and inferior gemellus.

items.why: Sartorius: flexes hip and knee, abducts and laterally rotates thigh; femoral n.

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the sartorius?
questions.explain: The femoral nerve innervates the quadriceps femoris, sartorius, and most of the iliacus.

questions.q: Which combination of actions does the sartorius perform?
choices: Extends hip and knee; adducts, medially rotates thigh
Flexes hip, extends knee; adducts, laterally rotates thigh
Flexes hip and knee; abducts, laterally rotates thigh
Extends hip, flexes knee; abducts, medially rotates thigh
questions.explain: The sartorius flexes the hip and knee and assists with abduction and lateral rotation of the thigh.

items.excerpt: The sartorius also flexes the hip and knee and assists with abduction and lateral rotation of the thigh.

items.why: Rectus femoris: crosses hip and knee; knee extension + hip flexion

questions.q: Which quadriceps muscle also flexes the hip because it crosses both the hip and knee joints?
questions.explain: Only the rectus femoris crosses both joints, so it extends the knee and also assists hip flexion; the vasti act only at the knee.

items.excerpt: Because the rectus femoris crosses both the hip and knee joints, it also contributes to hip flexion.

items.why: Vasti: knee extension (quadriceps); femoral n.

questions.q: What is the action of the vastus lateralis, medialis, and intermedius?
choices: Flexion of the leg at the knee
Flexion of the thigh at the hip
Adduction of the thigh at the hip
Extension of the leg at the knee
questions.explain: The three vasti, with rectus femoris, form the quadriceps femoris, the primary extensor of the knee.

items.excerpt: The quadriceps femoris is the primary extensor of the knee, and consists of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius.

items.why: Femoral n.: quadriceps, sartorius, iliacus; injury weakens knee extension +/- hip flexion

questions.q: A patient cannot extend the knee after injury to a major nerve of the thigh. Which additional finding is most consistent?
questions.explain: Weak knee extension points to the femoral nerve, which also supplies sartorius and most of iliacus, so hip flexion may be impaired.

items.excerpt: Injury to the femoral nerve therefore weakens knee extension and may also impair hip flexion.

items.why: Adductors: adduct thigh (longus/brevis assist flexion); obturator n.

questions.q: Adductor longus and brevis adduct the thigh and also assist with which hip movement?
questions.explain: Per Table 3, adductor longus and brevis adduct the thigh and assist with hip flexion (obturator nerve).

questions.q: A muscle in the medial compartment of the thigh most likely has which action and innervation?
questions.explain: The medial compartment primarily adducts the thigh and is innervated primarily by the obturator nerve.

items.excerpt: The muscles of the medial thigh compartment primarily adduct the thigh at the hip and receive innervation primarily from the obturator nerve.

items.why: Adductor magnus: adductor part (obturator n.) vs hamstring part (tibial division)

questions.q: The hamstring part of the adductor magnus is innervated by which nerve?
choices: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve
Common fibular division of sciatic nerve
questions.explain: The hamstring part of adductor magnus extends the thigh and is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: The adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explain: The adductor part adducts the thigh and is innervated by the obturator nerve, reflecting the muscle's dual function.

items.excerpt: Its hamstring part extends the thigh and receives innervation from the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.

items.why: Gracilis: crosses hip and knee; adducts thigh, flexes and medially rotates leg; obturator n.

questions.q: Besides adducting the thigh, the gracilis assists with which movement at the knee?
choices: Extension and lateral rotation of the leg
Flexion and lateral rotation of the leg
Extension and medial rotation of the leg
Flexion and medial rotation of the leg
questions.explain: The gracilis crosses the hip and knee: it adducts the thigh and assists with flexion and medial rotation of the leg at the knee.

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the gracilis?
questions.explain: The gracilis, like the adductors, is innervated by the obturator nerve.

items.excerpt: …In addition to adducting the thigh, it assists with flexion and medial rotation of the leg at the knee.

items.why: Pectineus: transitional anterior/medial muscle; usually femoral n.

questions.q: The pectineus is usually innervated by which nerve?
questions.explain: Pectineus is transitional between the anterior and medial compartments and is usually innervated by the femoral nerve.

items.excerpt: Pectineus is a transitional muscle between the anterior and medial compartments and is usually innervated by the femoral nerve.

items.why: Obturator n.: medial compartment adductors, gracilis, obturator externus

questions.q: Injury to the obturator nerve would most weaken which movement?
questions.explain: The obturator nerve supplies the medial compartment, whose dominant action is adduction of the thigh.

questions.q: Which deep lateral rotator of the hip would also be weakened by an obturator nerve injury?
questions.explain: Obturator externus is the deep rotator innervated by the obturator nerve; the others receive sacral plexus branches.

items.excerpt: The medial compartment primarily adducts the thigh and is innervated primarily by the obturator nerve.

items.why: Semitendinosus: ischial tuberosity; extends hip, flexes knee, medially rotates flexed leg

questions.q: Which posterior thigh muscle medially rotates the flexed leg?
questions.explain: Semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially rotate the flexed leg, while the biceps femoris laterally rotates it.

questions.q: The semitendinosus originates from which landmark?
questions.explain: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris originate from the ischial tuberosity.

items.excerpt: In addition to extending the thigh and flexing the knee, the semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially rotate the flexed leg…

items.why: Semimembranosus: ischial tuberosity; tibial division

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the semimembranosus?
choices: Common fibular division of the sciatic nerve
Tibial division of the sciatic nerve
questions.explain: Semimembranosus, like semitendinosus and the long head of biceps femoris, is innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.

items.excerpt: The semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of the biceps femoris originate from the ischial tuberosity and are innervated by the tibial division…

items.why: Biceps femoris long head: ischial tuberosity; laterally rotates flexed leg; tibial division

questions.q: Which rotation does the biceps femoris produce when the knee is flexed?
questions.explain: The biceps femoris laterally rotates the flexed leg; semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially rotate it.

questions.q: The long head of the biceps femoris is innervated by which nerve?
choices: Common fibular division of sciatic nerve
questions.explain: The long head arises from the ischial tuberosity and is supplied by the tibial division; the short head gets the common fibular division.

items.excerpt: …while the biceps femoris laterally rotates the flexed leg.

items.why: Biceps femoris short head: arises from femur, acts only at knee; common fibular division

questions.q: Which posterior thigh muscle is innervated by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve?
questions.explain: The short head of biceps femoris is the exception in the posterior thigh: common fibular division rather than tibial division.

questions.q: Why does the short head of the biceps femoris act only at the knee?
choices: It inserts proximal to the knee
It is supplied by the tibial division
questions.explain: The short head arises from the femur rather than the ischial tuberosity, so it does not cross the hip and acts only at the knee.

items.excerpt: The short head of the biceps femoris … acts only at the knee, and receives innervation from the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve.

items.why: Sciatic n.: exits below piriformis; supplies posterior compartment

questions.q: Which thigh compartment is innervated primarily by the sciatic nerve?
questions.explain: Anterior = femoral nerve, medial = obturator nerve, posterior = sciatic nerve.

items.excerpt: The posterior compartment primarily flexes the knee and extends the hip and receives innervation primarily through the sciatic nerve.

items.why: Tibial division: semitendinosus, semimembranosus, BF long head, hamstring part of adductor magnus

questions.q: A lesion confined to the tibial division of the sciatic nerve would spare which posterior thigh muscle?
questions.explain: The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common fibular division, so a tibial-division lesion spares it.

items.excerpt: The semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of the biceps femoris … are innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.

items.why: Common fibular division: biceps femoris short head
items.excerpt: It originates from the femur, acts only at the knee, and receives innervation from the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve.

items.why: Femoral condyles articulate with tibial condyles

questions.q: The medial and lateral condyles of the femur articulate with which structures?
choices: Head and neck of the fibula
questions.explain: The femoral condyles articulate with the corresponding condyles of the proximal tibia; the fibula does not join the knee joint.

items.excerpt: At the distal femur, the medial condyle and lateral condyle articulate with the corresponding condyles of the proximal tibia.

items.why: Patellar surface: anterior, between condyles, articulates with patella

questions.q: Which part of the distal femur articulates with the patella?
questions.explain: The patellar surface lies anteriorly between the femoral condyles and articulates with the patella.

items.excerpt: The patellar surface lies anteriorly between the femoral condyles and articulates with the patella.

items.why: Intercondylar fossa separates the condyles posteriorly
items.excerpt: Posteriorly, the condyles are separated by the intercondylar fossa.

items.why: Tibia: weight-bearing articulation at the knee
items.excerpt: The knee connects the thigh and leg through articulations among the femur, tibia, and patella.

items.why: Tibial condyles bear weight transmitted across the knee

questions.q: Through which structures does the proximal tibia bear the weight transmitted across the knee?
questions.explain: The proximal tibia bears weight through its medial and lateral condyles, which articulate with the femoral condyles.

items.excerpt: The proximal tibia bears the weight transmitted across the knee through its medial condyle and lateral condyle.

items.why: Intercondylar eminence: central attachment region for stabilizing structures
items.excerpt: Between these articular surfaces is the intercondylar eminence, which contributes to the central region where important stabilizing structures of the knee attach.

items.why: Tibial tuberosity: patellar ligament attachment
items.excerpt: Anteriorly, the tibial tuberosity provides attachment for the patellar ligament.

items.why: Patella: embedded in quadriceps tendon; links quadriceps to tibia

questions.q: The patella is embedded within which structure?
questions.explain: The patella is embedded within the quadriceps tendon and connects to the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.

items.excerpt: The patella is embedded within the quadriceps tendon and connects inferiorly to the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament

items.why: Fibula: adjacent to knee, not part of knee joint

questions.q: Which bone lies adjacent to the knee but does not participate directly in the knee joint?
questions.explain: The knee joint is formed by the femur, tibia, and patella; the fibula lies adjacent but does not participate.

items.excerpt: The fibula lies adjacent to the knee but does not participate directly in the knee joint.

items.why: Quadriceps tendon: contains the patella
items.excerpt: This arrangement links the quadriceps femoris to the tibia and allows force generated by the anterior thigh to be transmitted across the knee.

items.why: Patellar ligament: patella to tibial tuberosity

questions.q: The patellar ligament connects the patella to which landmark?
questions.explain: The patella connects inferiorly to the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament, transmitting quadriceps force to the tibia.

items.excerpt: The patella … connects inferiorly to the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament

items.why: Menisci: congruency, shock absorption, weight distribution; medial meniscus attached to MCL

questions.q: What is a main function of the medial and lateral menisci?
choices: Resist valgus stress on the knee
questions.explain: The fibrocartilaginous menisci improve congruency, absorb shock, and distribute weight; the cruciates and collaterals limit translation and varus/valgus.

items.excerpt: The menisci improve joint congruency, absorb shock, and distribute weight across the knee.

items.why: ACL limits anterior tibial translation; unhappy triad

questions.q: Disruption of the anterior cruciate ligament would most affect which displacement?
questions.explain: The ACL limits anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur.

items.excerpt: The ACL limits anterior translation of the tibia, while the PCL limits posterior translation.

items.why: PCL limits posterior tibial translation

questions.q: Which ligament limits posterior translation of the tibia?
questions.explain: The PCL limits posterior translation of the tibia; the ACL limits anterior translation.

items.excerpt: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) cross within the joint … limiting anterior and posterior translation of the tibia, respectively.

items.why: MCL resists valgus (attached to medial meniscus), LCL resists varus; unhappy triad

questions.q: Which ligament resists valgus stress at the knee?
questions.explain: The MCL resists valgus stress, a force driving the knee medially; the LCL resists varus stress.

questions.q: A soccer player with a planted foot is struck on the lateral knee, producing a strong valgus force. Which structures are classically injured?
questions.explain: A valgus force can injure the ACL, MCL, and medial meniscus (unhappy triad), reflecting the MCL's attachment to the medial meniscus.

items.excerpt: The MCL is attached to the medial meniscus, an anatomical relationship with important clinical consequences.

bricks.title: Vasculature and Lymphatics of the Lower Extremities (Gluteal & Thigh list)

items.why: Common iliac aa.: aortic bifurcation at L4; PAD can block them

questions.q: At what vertebral level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate into the common iliac arteries?
questions.explain: The abdominal aorta divides at the level of L4 into the right and left common iliac arteries.

questions.q: A patient has buttock and leg pain while climbing stairs that is relieved by rest; imaging shows a blocked common iliac artery. Diagnosis?
questions.explain: Atherosclerosis of lower extremity arteries causes peripheral artery disease with claudication: exertional pain relieved by rest.

items.excerpt: The abdominal aorta divides at the level of L4 into the right and left common iliac arteries

items.why: Internal iliac: pelvis, gluteal region, medial thigh; external iliac continues into limb

questions.q: Which artery gives rise to the superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, and obturator arteries?
questions.explain: The internal iliac artery gives the superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, and obturator arteries to the lower extremity.

questions.q: What does the internal iliac artery supply?
choices: Anterior thigh, knee, and proximal leg
Pelvis, gluteal region, and medial thigh
questions.explain: The internal iliac artery supplies the pelvis, gluteal region, and medial thigh compartment muscles.

items.excerpt: Each common iliac artery divides into an internal iliac artery, which supplies the pelvis and gluteal region, and an external iliac artery…

items.why: Superior gluteal a.: trochanteric anastomosis; inferior gluteal a.: cruciate anastomosis

questions.q: Branches of which artery join the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries to form the trochanteric anastomosis?
questions.explain: The circumflex femoral arteries and branches of the superior gluteal artery form the trochanteric anastomosis around the femoral neck.

questions.q: The cruciate anastomosis connects the circumflex femoral and first perforating arteries with which artery?
questions.explain: Posterior to the proximal femur near the lesser trochanter, the cruciate anastomosis links the inferior gluteal artery with the circumflex femoral and first perforating arteries.

items.excerpt: The major branches relevant to the lower extremity are the superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, and obturator arteries.

items.why: Obturator a.: internal iliac branch to medial thigh
items.excerpt: The internal iliac artery supplies the pelvis and gives rise to branches that supply the gluteal region and medial thigh compartment.

items.why: Inguinal ligament: external iliac becomes femoral a.; GSV joins femoral v. just below

questions.q: The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery as it passes which structure?
questions.explain: After passing deep to the inguinal ligament, the external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery.

items.excerpt: The external iliac artery passes beneath the inguinal ligament, where it becomes the femoral artery

items.why: Femoral a.: main supply of thigh; catheterization site, compress against femoral head

questions.q: Why is the femoral artery commonly used for arterial catheterization?
choices: It lies deep and is well protected
It has no accompanying vein or nerve
It passes through the adductor hiatus
It is large, superficial, and accessible
questions.explain: The femoral artery is large, superficial, and readily accessible, allowing catheters to be advanced into the aorta and coronary arteries.

questions.q: After a femoral catheter is removed, bleeding is controlled by compressing the artery against which structure?
questions.explain: Because the femoral artery can be compressed against the femoral head, bleeding can usually be controlled after catheter removal.

items.excerpt: The femoral artery is commonly used for arterial catheterization because it is large, superficial, and readily accessible.

items.why: Deep femoral a.: largest femoral branch; gives circumflex and perforating aa.

questions.q: What is the largest branch of the femoral artery?
questions.explain: The deep femoral artery (profunda femoris) is the largest branch of the femoral artery.

questions.q: Which arteries arise from the deep femoral artery?
questions.explain: The deep femoral artery gives rise to the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries and several perforating arteries.

items.excerpt: The largest branch of the femoral artery is the deep femoral artery (profunda femoris)…

items.why: Perforating aa.: supply most of the posterior thigh; first joins cruciate anastomosis

questions.q: Which vessels supply most of the posterior compartment of the thigh?
questions.explain: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery supply most of the posterior thigh; the femoral artery supplies the anterior thigh.

items.excerpt: The femoral artery supplies the anterior thigh, while the perforating arteries supply most of the posterior compartment of the thigh.

items.why: Adductor hiatus: femoral a. becomes popliteal a.

questions.q: Foot drop from common fibular nerve injury produces which compensatory gait?
questions.explain: Patients with foot drop lift the knee higher than normal (steppage gait) to keep the toes from dragging.

items.excerpt: Injury to the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck affects both its deep and superficial branches.

items.why: Deep fibular n.: anterior compartment; first dorsal web space

questions.q: A patient has numbness in the first dorsal web space but normal sensation over the rest of the dorsum. Which nerve is affected?
questions.explain: The deep fibular nerve supplies the first dorsal web space; intact sensation elsewhere on the dorsum means the superficial fibular nerve is spared.

items.excerpt: In contrast, an isolated deep fibular nerve injury primarily affects dorsiflexion and toe extension, with sensory loss limited to the first dorsal web space.

items.why: Superficial fibular n.: lateral compartment (eversion); most of dorsum of foot

questions.q: Which nerve supplies sensation to most of the dorsum of the foot?
questions.explain: The superficial fibular nerve supplies most of the dorsum of the foot; the deep fibular nerve supplies only the first dorsal web space.

questions.q: An isolated superficial fibular nerve injury would weaken which movement?
questions.explain: The superficial fibular nerve supplies the lateral compartment (fibularis longus and brevis), the main evertors.

items.excerpt: …whereas the superficial fibular nerve innervates the lateral compartment and supplies most of the dorsum of the foot.

items.why: Tibial n.: posterior compartment; tarsal tunnel; plantar sensation

questions.q: A patient has normal dorsiflexion and eversion but numbness limited to the plantar surface of the foot. Which nerve is affected?
questions.explain: Plantar sensation comes from the tibial nerve via the medial and lateral plantar nerves; normal dorsiflexion and eversion spare the fibular nerves.

questions.q: A tibial nerve lesion in the posterior leg would most impair which movements?
questions.explain: The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment, so a lesion above the ankle impairs plantarflexion and toe flexion.

items.excerpt: …passes through the tarsal tunnel posterior to the medial malleolus before dividing into the medial and lateral plantar nerves.

items.why: Medial and lateral plantar nn.: tibial branches; plantar intrinsics and plantar sensation

questions.q: Which nerve innervates most of the intrinsic muscles of the plantar foot?
questions.explain: Most plantar intrinsics are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve; abductor hallucis, FHB, FDB, and the first lumbrical are medial plantar.

items.excerpt: These branches provide motor innervation to the plantar intrinsic muscles and sensory innervation to the plantar surface of the foot.

items.why: Sural n.: posterolateral leg and lateral foot

questions.q: Sensory loss over the posterolateral leg and lateral foot suggests injury to which nerve?
questions.explain: The sural nerve supplies the posterolateral leg and lateral foot.
